query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a very low atomic‐loading of platinum as atomically dispersed sites onto the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive catalyst will enhance low‐temperature oxidation activity, suppress poisoning (e.g., CO, H2O, and NO adsorption), and improve long‐term durability by stabilizing the active surface through high‐entropy interactions—without significantly increasing platinum use.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst (e.g., a high‐entropy alloy-type catalyst already exhibiting mixed elemental sites and modest low-temperature oxidation activity).
generation.intervention: A controlled surface modification that deposits a sub-monolayer (atomic-scale) amount of platinum onto the catalyst, promoting its atomic dispersion within the existing high-entropy matrix through a thermal treatment that anchors the Pt atoms without forming larger nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Catalytic operation under simulated automotive exhaust conditions, including transient low temperatures (below 150 °C), exposure to water vapor and NO (as poisoning agents), and thermal aging (e.g., up to 850 °C for short cycles) to mimic real-driving-emission degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomically dispersed Pt sites that are strongly anchored by the high configurational disorder of the multi-principal-element matrix; the high-entropy environment prevents sintering and maintains dispersion while tuning the local electronic structure.
generation.mechanism: The dispersed Pt atoms modify the local coordination environment and electronic structure of the catalyst surface. This adjustment weakens the binding of poisoning species (such as CO and H2O) and facilitates the activation of oxygen and hydrocarbon molecules, thereby lowering the light-off temperature for oxidation. The high-entropy matrix confers resistance to sintering and thermal degradation, thereby prolonging catalyst lifetime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the Pt-doped catalyst should exhibit a significant reduction in the temperature required for complete CO and hydrocarbon oxidation (e.g., a decrease in T50 by at least 15–20 °C), demonstrably lower deactivation rates under hydrothermal conditions, and prolonged stability under cyclic aging—all while using only a minimal additional amount of platinum.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst shows higher activation temperatures, is more susceptible to deactivation by poisoning species, and exhibits faster deterioration under high-temperature aging cycles.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to be most pronounced under typical automotive exhaust conditions (transient low to moderate temperatures with water and NO presence and thermal cycling up to around 850 °C). Effects outside these conditions (e.g., extremely reductive atmospheres or ultra-high temperatures leading to support collapse) are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum Pt loading and specific dispersion state necessary to balance activity, poisoning resistance, and durability without excess cost remain to be fully determined. In addition, long-term behavior under real-world driving conditions and the interaction between Pt sites and specific poisoning species require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: (1) the unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy catalyst and (2) the same catalyst modified by an atomic-scale, low-loading Pt deposition followed by controlled thermal treatment. Subject both sets to standardized catalytic oxidation tests under simulated automotive exhaust conditions (including low-temperature operation, water vapor/NO exposure, and accelerated aging cycles).
measurements: Light-off temperatures (e.g., T50 for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation) under dry and humid conditions.
Catalyst stability metrics (e.g., percentage decline in activity over a predetermined aging period).
Surface characterization (e.g., HAADF-STEM, XPS) to verify Pt dispersion and absence of sintering.
Poisoning-resistance tests by monitoring conversion efficiency in the presence of CO, H2O, and NO.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Pt-modified catalyst does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least a 15–20 °C decrease in T50) in oxidation temperature, improved resistance to poisoning (maintaining conversion efficiency under poisoning conditions), and lower degradation rates compared to the baseline unmodified catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation. The catalytic performance of Pd1@HEFO is comparable to Pt/CeO2–SiAlOx regarded as a candidate of diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC) and Pt/CeO2. Moreover, no obvious deactivation of CO, C3H6, and NO oxidation can be observed over Pd1@HEFO even after 10 h of reaction in Supplementary Fig. 14b, implying that Pd1@HEFO shows a good DOC activity and stability. PXRD patterns of Pd1@HEFO treated in H2 at different temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 15) suggest that Pd atoms in Pd1@HEFO are not stable in reductive atmosphere. As a result, our Pd1@HEFO is more suitable for the oxidation reaction under the oxygen-rich conditions, such as catalytic destruction of pollutions emitted from diesel engines. These illustrate that our Pd1@HEFO possesses not only outstanding low-temperature CO oxidation activity but also excellent resistance to hydrothermal degradation as a candidate of DOC, thus possibly tolerating the harsh conditions during exhaust treatment of diesel engines.
